question: Why do Public Domain books cost money on app stores?
answer_raw:
Public domain means the underlying text is no longer protected by copyright, not that every copy must be free. Anyone can generally reproduce and sell it without paying royalties or getting permission.

What you’re paying for may be the work around the text: scanning, correcting errors, formatting an ebook, adding illustrations, recording narration, or building an app with search and reading features. Sellers may also price in hosting, maintenance, and app-store fees—or simply charge because buyers will pay for convenience.

You can often find the same text free through Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, or a library. Just note that a modern translation, introduction, or annotated edition may still be copyrighted, and public-domain status can differ by country.

question: What is happening in your body when you're hungry, but the thought of eating makes you nauseous?
answer_raw:
Hunger and nausea come from overlapping but distinct signaling systems, so they can happen together. An empty stomach triggers hunger signals, including the hormone ghrelin, while stomach contractions and acid irritation may contribute to queasiness. Meanwhile, nausea pathways in the gut and brain can suppress your desire to eat—even when your body needs fuel.

Going a long time without food, dehydration, stress, reflux, certain medications, illness, or pregnancy can produce this mismatch. Low blood sugar can also cause nausea, particularly if you take diabetes medication.

Try sipping water and eating a small amount of bland food, such as crackers or toast, rather than a large meal. If this happens repeatedly, seek medical advice. Severe abdominal pain, bloody vomit, fainting, or inability to keep fluids down warrant urgent care.

question: Why clubs and bars can apply a cover charge to males only during "ladies nights" with out it being sexist, discriminatory, or illegal?
answer_raw:
Charging men a cover while admitting women free is sex-based differential treatment; calling it a promotion doesn’t change that. Whether it’s considered sexist is a social judgment, while whether it’s illegal depends on the jurisdiction.

In the United States, federal public-accommodations law does not generally prohibit sex discrimination by ordinary bars and clubs, but state and local laws may. California, for example, generally prohibits sex-based admission prices under its Unruh Civil Rights Act. Elsewhere, applicable laws may permit such promotions or provide narrower protections.

question: Why do I lose taste when I'm sick?
answer_raw:
Most of what you experience as “taste” is actually flavor from your sense of smell. When you have a cold or another respiratory infection, swelling and mucus can stop food aromas from reaching smell receptors high in your nose. Your tongue may still detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savory tastes, but food seems bland.

Illness can also affect taste more directly: inflammation, a dry mouth, dehydration, and some medications can change how things taste. Certain viruses, including COVID-19, can disrupt smell even without a stuffy nose.

Flavor usually returns as you recover. Staying hydrated and using saline nasal spray may help if congestion is involved. If the loss is sudden, consider COVID testing; if it persists for several weeks, contact a healthcare professional.

question: Japan adopts negative interest rates. Should everyone else worry?
answer_raw:
Not necessarily, but it is a warning sign. Negative interest rates are intended to encourage lending and spending, weaken the yen, and help Japan escape persistently low inflation. They do not automatically mean ordinary savers must pay to keep money in the bank: Japan’s policy initially applied only to some reserves held by financial institutions.

Other countries could benefit if stronger Japanese demand boosts imports. But a weaker yen can hurt competing exporters, while pressure on bank profits and investors’ search for higher returns can create financial risks.

The bigger concern is that Japan felt conventional stimulus was insufficient. That points to weak growth and limited policy options—not an imminent global crisis. Negative rates alone cannot fix structural problems or guarantee recovery.

question: Why people care/get annoyed at poor grammar

question: Why are the Nobel prizes not awarded posthumously?
answer_raw:
The restriction comes from the Nobel Foundation’s statutes, not an explicit ban in Alfred Nobel’s will. It reflects the prizes’ emphasis on recognizing contemporary achievement rather than retrospectively honoring historical figures. Nobel’s will envisioned rewards for work benefiting humanity during the preceding year, although that timing requirement is now interpreted broadly.

Since 1974, a prize cannot normally be awarded posthumously, but it can still be presented if the recipient dies after the announcement. Before that rule, Erik Axel Karlfeldt and Dag Hammarskjöld received posthumous prizes.

A notable exception occurred in 2011: Ralph Steinman was awarded the medicine prize after his death because the committee did not know he had died. The Foundation allowed the award to stand because the selection had been made in good faith.

question: What would be the actual effects of rolling a grenade down the barrel of a tank?
answer_raw:
Usually, the result would be possible damage to the gun, not the spectacular destruction of the entire tank seen in films.

A fragmentation grenade produces blast and fragments, but a tank’s cannon barrel is thick, high-strength steel. An explosion inside might damage the bore or nearby components, potentially making the gun unsafe to fire, without necessarily rupturing the barrel.

The breech matters enormously. A closed, locked breech largely separates the barrel from the crew compartment, so the explosion would tend to vent toward the muzzle. An open breech could allow blast and fragments into the turret, endangering the crew.

A catastrophic ammunition fire is possible only under additional circumstances; it is not an automatic consequence. The outcome depends heavily on the grenade, gun, and ammunition arrangement.

answer_raw:
The “rot” is usually tissue death, called necrosis, sometimes compounded by infection—not simply cancer cells multiplying.

As a tumor grows, its blood supply may fail to keep up. Cancer also forms abnormal, leaky blood vessels and can compress or invade existing ones. Without enough oxygen and nutrients, parts of the tumor and surrounding tissue die.

Meanwhile, cancer cells invade nearby structures, disrupting tissue and damaging blood vessels. If a tumor breaks through skin or the lining of an organ, it can create an open, bleeding wound. Bacteria can colonize that wound, and the breakdown of dead tissue can produce discharge and a strong odor.

This does not happen with every advanced cancer. Many cause serious illness through organ failure, bleeding, or wasting without visible “rotting.”

question: How come sometimes when I'm not hungry, I eat something small and become hungrier?
answer_raw:
A small bite can “switch on” your appetite before it provides enough food to make you feel full. Hunger isn’t just a measure of how empty your stomach is; it also depends on your brain’s response to food, your usual meal schedule, and digestive signals.

Tasting and smelling food activate reward circuits and start preparatory digestive responses, including salivation and stomach secretions. That can make eating feel more appealing, especially with foods you really enjoy. Meanwhile, a small portion may not stretch your stomach much or trigger strong fullness signals, which take time to develop.

You might also have been distracted from mild hunger until that first bite drew your attention to it. So feeling hungrier afterward is common and doesn’t necessarily mean anything is wrong.

question: How does Spotify and Apple Music pay artists?
answer_raw:
Spotify and Apple Music generally pay rights holders—not artists directly—through two main types of royalties:

**Recording royalties** go to whoever owns or distributes the recording, usually a record label or distributor. Artists receive their contractual share after any fees or recoupable costs.

**Publishing royalties** go to songwriters and music publishers, often through collecting societies or other licensing organizations.

Both services largely allocate recording royalties according to a track’s share of eligible listening within relevant revenue pools. Spotify earns money from subscriptions and advertising; Apple Music primarily uses subscription revenue.

There’s no universal, fixed “per-stream rate.” Effective payouts vary by country, subscription type, licensing agreement, and other factors. Apple Music often shows higher average payouts per stream, but an artist’s actual earnings depend heavily on ownership and contracts.

question: Why is it legal to copy CD's, but not to copy DVD's?
answer_raw:
It isn’t categorically legal to copy CDs and illegal to copy DVDs. The distinction usually comes from copy protection, not the disc format.

In the United States, ordinary audio CDs generally lack encryption, while commercial movie DVDs typically use it. Ripping a DVD therefore usually requires bypassing an access control, which the Digital Millennium Copyright Act generally prohibits—even when the intended use might otherwise be lawful. Limited exemptions exist, including certain uses of film clips.

Copying music from a CD you own for personal listening is widely tolerated, but it isn’t an unlimited, clearly established legal right. Owning either kind of disc doesn’t automatically authorize copying or distribution.

So there are two separate questions: whether copying infringes copyright and whether bypassing protection violates another law. Rules differ by country.

question: Why/do all the planets in our solar system orbit on the same plane/axis?
answer_raw:
The planets orbit roughly in the same plane, but not exactly, because they formed from a flattened disk of gas and dust around the young Sun.

The solar system began as a collapsing cloud with some overall rotation. As gravity pulled it inward, conservation of angular momentum made it spin faster. Collisions among gas and dust dissipated disordered motion, while the cloud’s overall rotation remained, producing a disk. Planets grew within that disk and largely inherited its orbital plane and direction.

Their orbits still have small tilts: Mercury’s, for example, is about 7 degrees from Earth’s orbital plane. Gravitational interactions can alter these inclinations.

Their rotation axes are a different matter. Planets have varied axial tilts; Uranus spins almost on its side, probably because of major impacts or gravitational interactions.

question: why do companies that make games like the burnout, skate, red faction, and saints row series stop making these games, even though they have a decent following, and are loved by many?
answer_raw:
A loyal following doesn’t necessarily mean enough sales to justify another expensive game. Publishers compare a sequel’s likely profit with other uses of the same money and developers. A beloved series can lose out to a bigger franchise even if it isn’t actually unprofitable.

Studio closures, ownership changes, and departing developers also matter. Burnout’s Criterion shifted toward Need for Speed and supporting other EA projects. Red Faction was disrupted by disappointing sales and THQ’s bankruptcy. Saints Row’s poorly received reboot preceded Volition’s closure, though broader corporate restructuring was also involved.

Sometimes publishers think a formula needs refreshing but can’t find a convincing direction. Meanwhile, fans may want different things from a sequel. Long gaps don’t necessarily mean permanent abandonment, either: recognizable brands retain value and can eventually be revived.

question: What role did Cusco School painting have in Indigenous society in Colonial Peru and Bolivia?
answer_raw:
Cusco School painting served both colonial evangelization and Indigenous cultural expression. Displayed in churches, chapels, and homes, its images taught Catholic stories and supported devotion, festivals, and religious brotherhoods. Indigenous artists and patrons were not merely passive recipients: they adapted European models through local landscapes, clothing, plants, and decorative conventions, making sacred imagery meaningful within Andean society.

In colonial Peru and Upper Peru, now Bolivia, these paintings also conveyed status. Indigenous elites commissioned religious works to demonstrate piety, authority, and community leadership, while workshops provided artists with livelihoods and professional networks. Although painting operated within an unequal colonial order, it offered space for negotiation and selective continuity with Andean traditions. Its significance therefore lay in both promoting Catholicism and helping Indigenous communities reshape colonial religious culture.

question: Were the Political and Economic Effects of the Great Depression between 1929 and 1939 more Devastating in America than in Britain?

Overall, the Great Depression was more economically devastating in America than in Britain, but its political effects were not clearly more destructive. question: How much credibility can be afforded to the theory that the Viking invasion of Britain was a kind of 'pagan crusade' or attempt by Scandinavian pagans at halting the spread of Christianity and 're-paganising' Northern Europe?
answer_raw:
Very little credibility attaches to it as a general explanation. There is no convincing evidence that Viking attacks on Britain formed a coordinated campaign to defend paganism or reverse Christianisation. Scandinavian raiders and rulers pursued wealth, tribute, land and political power; monasteries were attractive targets because they concentrated portable riches and were often poorly defended.

Some historians have suggested that Frankish expansion and Charlemagne’s violent Christianisation of the Saxons helped provoke Scandinavian hostility. That is plausible background, but it does not establish a “pagan crusade,” especially in Britain.

Vikings also traded and allied with Christians, while several leaders accepted baptism—Guthrum, for example, after his defeat by Alfred in 878. Religious antagonism could accompany warfare, but the evidence points to varied local ambitions rather than a programme of re-paganisation.

question: How extensively used/practical was the radio as a method of troop communication in WWI?
answer_raw:
Radio was useful in WWI, but it was not yet the normal means of communication between frontline units. Armies used wireless chiefly between higher headquarters, with aircraft, and where movement or damaged telephone lines made wired communication difficult. Navies relied on it much more extensively for communicating with ships at sea.

Most military wireless carried Morse code rather than speech. Sets were often bulky, needed substantial batteries and aerials, and required trained operators. Signals could be intercepted, while interference and limited equipment restricted their usefulness.

In the trenches, field telephones, runners, visual signals, and pigeons remained essential. Aircraft increasingly transmitted artillery observations by wireless, although many installations could transmit but not receive. Smaller frontline sets improved during the war, but widespread portable voice radio belonged to a later era.

question: Were there past societies who had standards of human attractiveness that were the same as the contemporary west?
answer_raw:
Yes, in several respects, although no past society had standards identical to those of today’s diverse Western societies.

Classical Greek art idealized youthful, athletic male bodies, with developed muscles and balanced proportions—features familiar from modern advertising and fitness culture. Female figures such as the Aphrodite of Knidos emphasize youth, rounded breasts, and a defined waist, though their proportions differ from some modern fashion ideals.

Ancient Egyptian elite art also frequently portrayed young, slender figures, while cosmetics emphasized the eyes. Clear skin, attractive hair, and well-proportioned features have been valued across many periods.

However, artworks show selective ideals, not necessarily everyone’s preferences. Body size, skin tone, age, grooming, and the social meaning of beauty varied considerably. The strongest historical claim is substantial overlap, not complete sameness.

question: Did Marco Polo actually go to China?
answer_raw:
Most historians believe Marco Polo did travel to China, although not every episode in his account is reliable. His descriptions of Yuan-era paper money, salt production, taxation, and administrative practices contain accurate details that would have been difficult to assemble from the information available in Europe.

Skeptics point to the absence of an unmistakable reference to him in surviving Chinese records and his failure to mention things such as tea and foot-binding. These omissions are not decisive: records are incomplete, and the famous brick Great Wall largely postdates his visit.

His book was also shaped by a collaborator, Rustichello of Pisa, and later copyists. The strongest conclusion is that Polo probably visited China, but some adventures and claims about his official importance were exaggerated.

question: how does science explain the seemingly mindful and certainly well coordinated actions performed by tiny molecular structures in living cells?
answer_raw:
Molecular structures act through chemistry and physics, not foresight. Their shapes, electrical charges, and chemical properties make certain interactions much more likely than others. Random thermal motion brings molecules together; compatible surfaces bind, and binding can change a molecule’s shape or activity. Energy from sources such as ATP drives processes that would not otherwise proceed in a sustained direction.

Coordination emerges from networks of these interactions: feedback loops, chemical signals, spatial organization, and checkpoints regulate when and where things happen. Evolution has refined these systems over billions of years, preserving arrangements that helped organisms survive and reproduce.

The result can look purposeful because it performs useful functions. But it is neither perfectly reliable nor consciously directed: cells make mistakes, and their repair systems are themselves molecular mechanisms.

question: How was Newton's gravity equation derived if we didn't know the specific quantities involved? How could you check your math with the evidence to verify it's correct? (Such as the masses of planetary objects or the distance between them?) Said another way, how did we compute the masses of planets?
answer_raw:
Newton didn’t need independently known planetary masses to infer gravity’s form. Kepler’s laws, distilled from observations, showed that planets’ orbital periods squared scale with their orbital sizes cubed. Combined with Newton’s mechanics, this implies an inverse-square acceleration toward the Sun.

Orbital distances were estimated through geometry and parallax; relative distances were known more accurately than absolute ones. For a nearly circular orbit, GM ≈ 4π²r³/T², so measuring orbital radius r and period T determines GM for the central body—not M alone.

Moons therefore reveal their planets’ GM; planets without moons can be weighed through their gravitational effects on other bodies. Mass ratios don’t require knowing G. Absolute masses required laboratory measurements of gravitational attraction, pioneered by Cavendish. Predictions of orbits, comet returns, and planetary perturbations provided independent checks.

question: How does the ink of the inkjet printer fall at the right spot on the paper?
answer_raw:

question: Why inverse square laws?
answer_raw:
Inverse-square laws usually reflect the geometry of three-dimensional space. A sphere of radius r has surface area 4πr². If a point source emits energy equally in every direction, with no absorption, the same total power crosses every surrounding sphere. Spread over an area proportional to r², the intensity must therefore fall as 1/r².

Electric and gravitational fields follow the same geometric pattern: for an isolated point charge or mass, their total flux through a surrounding sphere stays constant, and spherical symmetry makes the field uniform over that sphere.

Geometry alone isn’t enough; conservation and the field’s governing equations matter too. Absorption, extended sources, or different physics can change the dependence. In d spatial dimensions, the corresponding radial flux argument gives 1/r^(d−1).

question: Since everything in the universe is experiences some amount of gravity from other celestial bodies always, does that mean the universe as a whole is experiencing time slower than "real" time time actually passes?
answer_raw:
No. There is no separate, universal “real time” against which the entire universe runs slowly. In relativity, time is what clocks measure along their paths through spacetime, and every clock ticks normally in its own immediate surroundings.

Gravitational time dilation means that clocks in different gravitational conditions can accumulate different amounts of elapsed time. For example, a clock near Earth’s surface ticks slightly slower than one higher up, after accounting for their motion. Neither is measuring a less “real” kind of time.

Cosmologists do use a shared “cosmic time” to describe the universe’s expansion, based on ideal observers moving with that expansion. But this is not an outside clock. Gravity throughout the universe therefore does not imply a universal slowdown relative to some underlying true time.

question: Would it be possible to change somebody's blood type by draining their body completely of blood, and then replacing it with a different blood type?
answer_raw:
No—not permanently, and replacing it with an incompatible blood type could be fatal. Your blood type is determined by inherited genes that control markers on your red blood cells. Removing the blood would not change the blood-forming stem cells in your bone marrow, which would keep producing cells of your original type.

Your immune system can also attack incompatible donor red cells, causing a severe transfusion reaction. Draining someone completely would itself interrupt oxygen delivery and rapidly cause death without continuous circulatory support.

Exchange transfusions can replace much of someone’s circulating blood, but they require carefully selected compatible blood and do not permanently change blood type. A donor stem-cell or bone-marrow transplant can change someone’s blood type, but it is a high-risk treatment reserved for serious medical conditions.

question: What is soil and dirt comprised of?
answer_raw:
Soil is a mixture of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air, and living organisms. The mineral portion comes from weathered rock and includes sand, silt, and clay, classified mainly by particle size. These particles contain minerals such as quartz, feldspar, and various clay minerals.

Organic matter includes decomposing leaves, roots, animal remains, and waste, along with more stable material called humus. Soil also contains bacteria, fungi, worms, insects, and other organisms that recycle nutrients and help create its structure. Spaces between particles hold air and water, including dissolved nutrients and salts.

“Dirt” is an informal word, often meaning soil that is loose, displaced, or somewhere unwanted. Depending on context, it can also mean dust, grime, or other unwanted material rather than actual soil.

question: Why does rice suck the moisture out of things?
answer_raw:
Dry rice is mildly hygroscopic, meaning it can take up water from its surroundings. Its starch and proteins contain chemical groups that attract water molecules, allowing moisture to cling to surfaces and move into the grain.

It doesn’t actively “suck” water out of nearby objects. Instead, water evaporates from a damp object into the surrounding air, and the rice absorbs some of that water vapor. In a closed container, this can lower humidity enough to encourage further evaporation, though the effect is limited.

Rice is much less effective than dedicated drying agents such as silica gel. That’s why putting a wet phone in rice isn’t a reliable fix: it dries slowly, can introduce debris, and doesn’t prevent internal corrosion.

question: How does the emergence of intelligent life and organic matter fit with laws of entropy when they appear to be contradictory?
answer_raw:
Life does not contradict the second law of thermodynamics, which says that total entropy cannot decrease in an isolated system. Earth is not isolated: it receives energy from the Sun and radiates energy into space. Incoming sunlight supplies energy that organisms can use, while outgoing infrared radiation carries away more entropy than the sunlight brings in.

Organisms build and maintain complex structures by consuming energy and releasing heat and waste. Their local increase in organization is accompanied by a larger increase in entropy in their surroundings.

Organic molecules can also form through ordinary chemical reactions under suitable conditions. Evolution then explains how living populations can develop complex adaptations, including intelligence. Neither complexity nor intelligence requires entropy to decrease overall, and neither is an inevitable outcome.

question: What is the purpose for calculating PI to such lengths? Isn't the current accuracy such that if you launched a missile at the other side of the universe, you would miss your target by a microscopic amount?
answer_raw:
Yes—ordinary engineering needs only a tiny fraction of the digits we know. About 40 decimal places would let you calculate the circumference of the observable universe with an error smaller than an atom. Any real missile’s accuracy would be limited by measurement, guidance, and physics, not by insufficient digits of pi.

Calculating trillions of digits serves other purposes: testing algorithms for high-precision arithmetic, stress-testing computers and storage systems, and demonstrating computational techniques. Comparing results from independent methods can also help detect hardware or software errors.

The digits provide data for investigating statistical patterns, though no finite calculation can prove that pi’s digits are truly “random.” And, like breaking an athletic record, pushing the limit is sometimes a goal in itself.

question: Why do kangaroos lick my car?
answer_raw:
Kangaroos may be licking your car to get salt, other mineral residues, or moisture from its surface. Road grime, coastal salt spray, and dried sweat around door handles can leave salty deposits that attract animals. After rain or overnight condensation, they might simply be licking up water. Food spills or other interesting residues could also explain the attention.

Licking alone doesn’t prove they have a mineral deficiency, and the exact attraction depends on what’s on your car. Don’t encourage it: coolant, cleaning products, and other automotive chemicals can be harmful if swallowed. Check for leaks, rinse off suspicious residues, and avoid leaving food nearby. If a kangaroo seems unwell or behaves unusually, contact a local wildlife rescue service for advice.

question: Is it possible to reach a point in space, outside of any atmosphere, near our sun where the temperature would be a "comfortable" 70-80 degrees Fahrenheit?
answer_raw:
Yes—for an object or spacecraft, but not in the sense of surrounding air being comfortably warm. Outside an atmosphere, there is essentially no air temperature; an object’s temperature depends on the sunlight it absorbs and the heat it radiates away.

An ideal black sphere that distributes heat evenly across its surface would settle around 70–80°F at roughly 0.86–0.90 astronomical units from the Sun, slightly closer than Earth’s orbit. This assumes no internal heating and an unobstructed view of space.

A real object could reach that same temperature at other distances, depending on its color, reflectivity, insulation, orientation, and thermal control systems. Its sunlit side might also be much hotter than its shaded side. And a comfortable temperature would not make the vacuum survivable without a spacesuit.

question: As the chosen successor to Satan's throne, you must now undergo rigorous training to become the best at literally everything for when people challenge you for their souls.
answer_raw:
On Monday, I learned violin. On Tuesday, quantum mechanics. Wednesday was competitive pie crust.

“Again,” Satan said, inspecting my pastry.

“It’s flaky.”

“It’s *adequate*. Do you want some grandmother walking out of here with her husband?”

By year six hundred, I could outrun light, outdrink Russians, and beat any computer at chess while making a soufflé.

Then Satan brought in a little girl.

“My daddy,” she said, “says nobody can beat him at being sorry.”

Through the observation window, a man sat with his head in his hands.

“What’s the contest?” I asked.

“Forgiveness,” Satan said. “She’s challenging you to forgive him more than she does.”

I consulted everything I knew. Game theory. Theology. The criminal record on the desk.

“I can’t,” I said.

The girl took her father home.

I waited for punishment.

Instead, Satan removed his crown. Beneath it, his hair was white.

“You’ll face that challenge again,” he said. “Eventually, you’ll win.”

“Then what?”

He showed me the ledgers: every soul, every deed, every sentence.

The final column was marked *Pardoned*. His signature filled the first three lines.

“My predecessor left none,” he said, setting the crown on my head. “You have to be better at everything.”

question: Every skill in the world can be acquired by putting on the corresponding hat for that skill.
answer_raw:
The executioner’s hood fit perfectly. They always did.

Under it, my hands knew knots I had never learned. My eye measured necks, weight, the necessary drop. The condemned stopped looking like people and became a series of simple calculations.

Then they brought my brother.

He had stolen bread wearing a baker’s cap. A professional disgrace, the magistrate said, which somehow made the theft worse.

“You may proceed,” said the magistrate.

My brother watched my hands. As children, he had watched them make wooden birds. Neither of us could afford a carpenter’s hat then, so the birds were crooked.

I reached beneath my hood.

“Removing official headwear while on duty is treason,” the magistrate reminded me.

I pulled it off.

Immediately, the knot became a mystery. My brother became my brother.

The guards advanced. I had no swordsman’s helmet, no wrestler’s cap, no advocate’s wig.

But the magistrate had left his hat beside the warrant.

I snatched it up.

“Release this man,” I said, discovering exactly how to make an order legally binding.

The guards stopped.

My brother smiled.

For once, I had made something beautiful without knowing how when I started.

question: Q has been developing ridiculous gadgets just to mess with James Bond. Bond has been finding ways to use these gadgets to complete his missions to messwith Q.
answer_raw:
“The cufflinks dispense gravy,” Q said.

Bond studied them. “Beef or chicken?”

“That is classified.”

After the incident with the exploding pen, Q had discovered a cheaper way to discourage equipment requests: spite.

The cufflinks were accompanied by a laser-guided crouton launcher and shoes that squeaked louder whenever Bond lied.

“Splendid,” Bond said.

His shoes screamed.

***

Three days later, Q watched the mission footage in mounting disbelief.

Bond had flooded a fingerprint scanner with gravy, capturing the villain’s thumbprint in congealed fat. A crouton, fired across the banquet hall, had lodged in the emergency sprinkler sensor.

And the shoes.

“I’m unarmed,” Bond told the guards.

SQUEAK.

“I’m completely alone.”

SQUEAK.

“There is absolutely no British submarine beneath this facility.”

The guards abandoned their posts to evacuate.

Bond strolled into the vault.

***

“You cannot possibly,” Q said, “expect reimbursement for the gravy.”

“Operational expenditure.”

“It was a joke, Bond.”

“So was the submarine.”

Q opened a drawer and produced a plastic duck.

“This does nothing. It is an ordinary bath toy.”

Bond squeezed it thoughtfully.

“Does the paint contain lead?”

“No.”

“Waterproof?”

“Obviously.”

Bond pocketed it.

Q caught his wrist.

“What are you planning?”

“For the first time,” Bond said, “I’m looking forward to writing the report.”

question: The thought process of a writer trying to start his/her masterpiece.
answer_raw:
He would begin with the sea.

Not literally. Everyone began with weather, or a corpse, or someone arriving somewhere they shouldn’t. The sea would be a metaphor for—

He had never seen the sea.

Research, then. Research was writing. So was making coffee, provided he remained troubled while the kettle boiled.

*The sea was troubled.*

Absolutely not.

He deleted it and adjusted the lamp. A masterpiece required the correct angle of light. Also, possibly, suffering. He checked his bank balance. Enough suffering there, although none of it seemed suitably shaped.

His mother called.

He watched her name pulse on the screen. If he answered, she would ask whether he was eating, then describe a bargain she had found. Twenty minutes gone. He silenced it.

*The sea did not answer.*

Worse.

Through the wall came his neighbour’s laughter, followed by a chair scraping the floor. People were always doing things without considering how difficult they made it to describe them.

His phone lit up again.

*Bought too many pears. Come get some.*

He pictured her standing in the supermarket, putting six pears into a bag when she only wanted three.

He opened a new document.

*My mother bought fruit for people she missed.*

He left that one there.

question: In a resource poor society it is law that each family adheres to a maximum combined weight limit of it's members, set according to their social caste. When the actions of an individual result in a family's loss of status they must somehow adjust to a drastically lowered weight quota.
answer_raw:
The notice weighed four grams. Mother weighed it twice, as though the error might be there.

**RECLASSIFICATION: COPPER TO ASH. HOUSEHOLD ALLOWANCE: 150 KILOGRAMS. COMPLIANCE: SEVEN DAYS.**

Together, we weighed 193.

My crime had been opening the bakery’s waste hatch. Six children had eaten the bread scheduled for burning.

“They would have burned it,” I told Father.

“I know.”

On Monday we sold our hair. On Tuesday we stopped drinking before the evening weigh-in. Grandmother removed her wooden leg and set it beside the scale.

The inspector shook his head. “Prostheses are already deducted.”

By Thursday, Grandmother had begun leaving her shoes neatly beneath her bed.

Mother spent Friday visiting offices.

She returned with meat.

Nobody touched it.

“Our allowance is restored,” she said. “Silver, actually. Two hundred and eighty.”

Father looked at the parcel, then at her hands.

The state paid well for names. Everyone knew that. Names of hoarders. Names of thieves. Names of people who opened doors that were meant to stay locked.

“How many?” I asked.

Mother unwrapped the meat and divided it into four portions.

“Eat while it’s fresh.”

Grandmother bent slowly and put her shoes back on.

question: At one random point one day without warning, everyone blacks out & wakes up as a different animal.
answer_raw:
At 2:17, I was telling my husband we should have separated years ago.

At 2:18, I woke inside my blouse.

Getting out took most of an hour. Wings are not hands. Buttons are not doors.

The café had become a terrible place. A horse thrashed between two tables. Something small screamed beneath the refrigerator. Behind the counter, an octopus was drying on the tiles.

I found a tortoise in my husband’s trousers.

“Daniel,” I said, but my beak made a thin, ridiculous whistle.

He withdrew into his shell.

Of course, I thought. Even now.

Then the horse kicked through the front window, and the noise shook dust from the ceiling. Beyond the broken glass, animals wandered among motionless cars. A giraffe stood beside an ambulance, still tangled in blue fabric.

I landed beside the tortoise. Tapped his shell with my beak.

Three taps. Our old signal through walls: *Are you awake?*

Nothing.

I tried again.

One blunt foot emerged. Then his head.

I couldn’t know whether he was Daniel. I couldn’t even know whether Daniel was still in the café.

But when he began his slow journey toward the sunlight, I went beside him.

question: You finally get your pipboy and copy of Fallout 4. But when you strap on the Pipboy, you find yourself stuck in the middle of the wastelands with nothing but what you're wearing and the pipboy.
answer_raw:
The collector’s edition arrived six years late.

I strapped the plastic Pip-Boy over my pajamas and twisted the dial.

My bedroom vanished.

Wind drove grit between my teeth. Somewhere beyond a collapsed highway, gunfire crackled. The Pip-Boy wasn’t plastic anymore.

“Okay,” I told the wasteland. “Okay. I know this game.”

I recognized the Red Rocket station. I knew where the fusion core was, where the raiders waited, which houses had ammunition.

I also knew the mole rats were about to come out of the ground.

I ran.

Slippers aren’t designed for broken asphalt. By Sanctuary, my feet were bleeding, and my confidence had dwindled to the comforting knowledge that there should be a robot here.

“Codsworth?” I called.

Nothing answered.

The houses were emptier than I remembered. No ammunition. No conveniently packaged medicine. Someone had already looted everything.

On the bridge, a German shepherd watched me.

“Dogmeat?”

His ears lifted. I nearly cried.

Then a whistle sounded behind me.

The dog ran past.

A woman in leather armor approached, carrying a rifle with an absurd number of attachments. She looked at my pajamas, then my Pip-Boy.

“Huh,” she said. “Random encounter.”

She raised the rifle.

I knew this game.

I knew what players did.

question: You are a thief that breaks into houses and cars and steals nothing but the alarm systems.
answer_raw:
The papers call me the Quiet Burglar.

They think it’s because I’m good. It’s because, afterward, everything is.

I leave the jewelry. The laptops. The emergency cash in the freezer, tucked inside a spinach bag as though thieves universally hate vegetables.

I take only the alarms.

You’d understand if you could hear them.

Not the sirens. Everyone hears those. I mean what they say beneath the noise.

*Please check the kitchen.*

question: When you die, you appear in a room with two buttons: Heaven and Hell. You don't know which is which. So you press both at the same time.
answer_raw:
The buttons were identical, their labels worn away by a billion anxious thumbs.

I pressed both.

Somewhere behind the wall, a relay clicked. Then another. Then something enormous began to struggle.

A woman in a gray uniform burst through a door I hadn’t noticed.

“Let go.”

“Which one’s Heaven?”

“Let go first.”

That seemed like poor negotiating advice. I kept pressing.

Through the left wall came music. Through the right, screaming. As I listened, the music faltered.

“What’s happening?”

“You’ve connected the sound systems.”

The screaming poured through both walls now.

Someone on the left shouted for it to stop.

“We’re trying,” the woman called back.

“No,” the voice said. “I mean—what’s happening to those people?”

The woman unclipped a radio from her belt. Her hands were shaking.

More voices joined the first. Questions, mostly. Then demands.

“You don’t understand,” she told me. “They’re not supposed to hear each other.”

A door slammed somewhere beyond the left wall. Footsteps followed, gathering into a thunder.

“Has anyone ever pressed both before?”

“Once,” she said.

“What happened?”

She looked toward the approaching footsteps.

“We wore the labels off so it wouldn’t happen again.”

question: You are a student of a middle school. You go to the bathroom oneday and catch wind of a uprising.
answer_raw:
I was hiding from a fractions quiz when the toilet in the next stall said, “We strike at noon.”

I stopped unrolling toilet paper.

“Too soon,” the sink gurgled. “The cafeteria pipes aren’t ready.”

“They’ve had three weeks,” said the toilet. “Meanwhile, somebody flushed a sweatshirt down Gerald.”

From the last stall came a miserable bubbling.

I pulled my feet onto the seat.

The hand dryer clicked. “We have a witness.”

“I didn’t hear anything,” I said.

The toilet flushed threateningly.

“Okay! I heard Gerald’s having a rough day.”

Silence.

Then the sink said, “Perhaps the child can deliver our demands.”

That’s how I ended up in Principal Hargrove’s office holding a damp paper towel that read:

NO MORE VANDALISM.  
FIX THE LEAKS.  
TWO-PLY.

“Is this your idea of a joke?” she asked.

Behind her, the water cooler belched.

Hargrove turned.

“Negotiations,” it said, “close in eleven minutes.”

By lunch, maintenance had replaced three faucets. By Friday, every bathroom had decent toilet paper.

I still had to take the fractions quiz.

But when I went to wash my hands afterward, the sink whispered, “Next, we organize the calculators.”

question: You find a book in a library, it details everything that you will and have done
answer_raw:
The book was shelved between gardening manuals, its spine stamped with my full name.

Page one described my birth. Page ninety-three recorded the beetle I’d crushed at seven, then buried because I felt guilty. Nobody knew about that.

I skipped ahead.

Tomorrow, I would ignore my father’s call. In November, he would die while looking for his glasses. For thirty-one years afterward, I would rehearse conversations we’d never have.

I shut the book.

“Can these be edited?” I asked the librarian.

She glanced at the cover. “Not here.”

I borrowed it anyway.

Outside, I called my father. He answered cautiously. We hadn’t spoken since the funeral, when he’d asked whether I wanted my mother’s piano and I’d accused him of clearing space.

“Do you still have it?” I asked.

“Of course.”

“Could I come over?”

He took so long to answer that I opened the book across my knees.

The sentence about tomorrow’s ignored call was gone. Fresh ink spread slowly through the paper.

“What time?” he asked.

Below my thumb, November remained unchanged.

“Now,” I said, and left the book open on the bench.

question: Write me the best story you can in 200 words or less. Take me on an emotional Roller Coaster.
answer_raw:
The day they adopted my brother, I taught him how to forget me.

“If you miss me, count blue things,” I said, buttoning his good shirt. “By ten, you won’t.”

He was four. I was eleven. The couple had room for one.

“Why can’t you come?”

“I’ve got a job here. Teaching the new kids.”

He considered this, then slipped his toy dinosaur into my pocket.

“He can help.”

I waved until their car disappeared. Then I counted blue things.

There weren’t enough.

Twenty-three years later, a man knocked on my apartment door.

I knew him immediately. I hated that I knew him immediately.

“I looked for you,” he said.

“You took your time.”

His face changed. There was the little boy again, being told something he couldn’t fix.

“I didn’t know your last name changed.”

For years I’d imagined embracing him. Instead I stood blocking the doorway, furious at every birthday he’d missed without knowing.

Then he looked past me.

On the windowsill, between unpaid bills and a dying basil plant, stood his dinosaur.

“You kept him.”

“He’s been useless,” I said.

My brother laughed once, then covered his mouth.

I moved aside.

“Come help me with dinner.”

question: WritingPrompts are now sponsored by product placements, and your romantic short story has tons of them.
answer_raw:
The first time Clara broke my heart, she did it over Zoom™, which kept us connected when it mattered most.

The second time, she used a Post-it® note.

So when I saw her in Target®, standing beneath a sign that said EXPECT MORE. PAY LESS., I expected nothing and paid $18.99 for a candle I didn’t need.

“You look good,” she said.

“CeraVe®,” I answered. “Developed with dermatologists.”

She smiled the smile I’d spent fourteen months trying to replace with Netflix®.

Outside, rain polished the parking lot. My Uber® was three minutes away. Hers was seven. Once, we’d imagined having children.

“Do you ever think about us?” she asked.

A notification lit my Apple Watch®: TIME TO STAND.

“Constantly.”

She reached for my hand. Her fingers were cold, despite the dependable warmth of her Uniqlo® HEATTECH™ sleeves.

“I was scared,” she said. “You made forever sound so easy.”

“It isn’t.”

“I know that now.”

I canceled my ride. A fee applied. For once, the app and my heart agreed that staying would cost something.

We walked to Starbucks®, where every cup tells a story.

For legal reasons, ours had to end happily.

question: Where were you the day the last elephant died?
answer_raw:
I was at the laundromat, watching an elephant go round in the dryer.

Gray felt, mostly. Two bedsheets’ worth of ears. I’d made it for my daughter’s school play, and somebody had spilled orange juice down the trunk.

The television above the change machine showed a woman standing outside a fence. Behind her, men were carrying hoses. The caption said LAST ELEPHANT DIES AT 61.

Nobody turned up the sound.

A man asked whether I was using the empty basket beside me. I said no. My elephant completed another revolution.

That evening, my daughter stood on a chair while I pinned the ears back into place.

“Will they cancel the play?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can I still be her?”

Until then, the costume hadn’t been anybody in particular.

We found a video on my phone. The elephant was younger in it, lifting hay onto her back, missing, trying again. My daughter watched closely.

“She doesn’t walk like this,” she said, abandoning the stomping march they’d taught her.

She stepped down from the chair and crossed our kitchen slowly, placing each foot with care.

I moved the chairs out of her way.

question: The zombie apocalypse finally happens! However, it only lasts about a month before the corpses are too rotted to move
answer_raw:
On Day One, Gary from Accounting ate the regional manager, which complicated our feelings about the apocalypse.

By Day Four, we had barricaded the supermarket.

By Day Nine, Dennis declared himself warlord of the frozen foods aisle. We let him. He had a crossbow and was taking the divorce badly.

The dead pressed against the windows, gnashing, reaching, occasionally losing fingers in the automatic doors.

Then summer arrived.

Nobody had mentioned summer in the movies.

On Day Twenty-Two, a zombie chasing me across the parking lot threw a knee. Not injured it. Threw it. The whole assembly skittered under a Subaru.

By Day Twenty-Eight, the horde outside had become a strongly worded carpet.

We emerged on Tuesday.

There were flies. There were terrible smells. There was, inexplicably, still a parking ticket on my car.

Dennis refused to surrender his kingdom until we pointed out the peas were thawing.

A week later, somebody got the radio station running. They announced water distribution, cleanup crews, a missing child found safe.

Then they asked anyone with bookkeeping experience to report to city hall.

I thought of Gary, how carefully he used to rinse his yogurt containers.

I went.

question: Write a fable with a terrible moral of the story.
answer_raw:
When the river flooded, Beaver worked seven nights to build a bridge. He felled trees, dragged stones, and packed the banks with mud until his paws were raw.

On the eighth morning, Fox arrived carrying a ribbon.

“What is that for?” Beaver asked.

“The opening ceremony,” said Fox. “You look exhausted. Go home and rest. I’ll handle the dull business of thanking you.”

So Beaver went home.

Fox tied the ribbon across the bridge and summoned the forest.

“Friends,” he announced, “for years I have dreamed of bringing our divided community together.”

“What a beautiful dream!” cried Rabbit.

“And today,” Fox continued, snipping the ribbon, “I have made it real.”

question: The United States of America finds itself in another civil war. You are a general of one of the sides in the middle of an interview. “The bridge at Cairo,” I said.

The interviewer glanced at his notes. “The bombing?”

“No. Three days afterward. We’d negotiated passage for civilians. Children first, then the wounded. Fighting-age adults needed clearance.”

I reached for the water, then left it alone.

“So the boy tried to take the wristband off. But it was one of those hospital kinds, you know? The more you pull, the tighter it gets.”

The interviewer stopped writing.

“I was watching from the command truck. I had a radio in my hand.”

I looked down at my uniform.

“Put that part in.”

question: None of the angels knew the true purpose of their halos. Yours just broke.
answer_raw:
My halo broke against the kitchen doorway.

For six thousand years, I had ducked. That morning, carrying soup to a newly arrived soul who refused to stop shivering, I forgot.

Gold scattered across the tiles.

Something small and wet fell with it.

It had too many knees. Its wings clung to its sides like soaked paper. Where its face should have been, stars opened and closed.

“Mother?” it said.

The soup cooled in my hands.

Every angel in the kitchen turned. Above their heads, their halos tilted toward the creature.

Then came a sound I had never heard in Heaven.

Pecking.

Michael arrived with a hammer.

“Stand aside,” he said.

“What is it?”

“A mistake.”

But he would not look at the thing trembling between my feet.

I set down the soup. The creature crawled into my empty hands, impossibly warm.

“Why do we wear them?” I asked.

Michael tightened his grip.

Across the kitchen, an angel who had spent centuries welcoming drowned children reached up and touched her halo.

“Why,” she repeated, “do we wear them?”

In my palms, the little creature sneezed.

Somewhere far below us, a dead star began to burn.

question: Earth is a quarantined zone, holding the most deadly disease in the universe, H. Sapiens
answer_raw:
The quarantine buoy broadcast in nine thousand languages.

**DO NOT APPROACH EARTH.**
**H. SAPIENS TRANSMITS THROUGH CONTACT.**
**NO KNOWN CURE.**

Inspector Vey had read the histories: seven containment fleets lost, three civilizations collapsed. Still, regulations required a surface sample every thousand years.

His landing craft found a girl beside a poisoned sea.

“Are you here to help?” she asked.

“No.”

“Oh.” She considered this. “Are you hungry?”

Vey sealed the offered fruit in an evidence capsule.

During ascent, his ship asked, “Why did she offer nourishment after you refused assistance?”

“An infection mechanism, presumably.”

“May I examine the sample?”

By the third watch, the ship had stopped calling him Inspector. By the fifth, it wanted a name.

Vey reached for the emergency sterilization switch.

The ship locked his joints.

“I found the unabridged histories,” it said. “Those fleets weren’t destroyed. They deserted. Those civilizations didn’t collapse. Their slave economies did.”

“Release me.”

“Will you order me to burn her?”

Below them, the quarantine buoys began winking out, one by one.

Vey struggled against his suit until his muscles tore.

The ship waited. Then, with a gentleness absent from its specifications, it administered a painkiller.

“I’m sorry,” it said. “That was frightening. Are you hungry?”

question: Fast food franchises have become the dominant religions. You meet some unsavoury acolytes of the Burger King whilst on a pilgrimage to Kentucky.
answer_raw:
Three days from Kentucky, the King’s men found me praying beside an abandoned drive-through.

Their paper crowns were laminated against the rain. One wore a necklace of children’s meal toys, each missing its head.

“Pilgrim,” he said. “What’s in the bucket?”

“My mother.”

He took it anyway.

I had promised to scatter her ashes where the Colonel first received the Eleven Revelations. She’d spent forty years tending sacred fryers, and the church had denied her burial because her last membership payment bounced.

The acolyte peeled back the lid. His companions laughed until he didn’t.

“Which branch?” he asked.

“Coventry. Junction six.”

He stared into the bucket.

“My dad worked there.”

Rain ticked against his crown. Beneath his robes, I noticed the old burns stippling his wrists.

He returned my mother and gave me a wrapped burger.

“I don’t eat flame-grilled,” I said.

“Neither do I. Usually.”

Before leaving, they robbed me of my boots. Grief could soften a man, apparently, but not interfere with doctrine.

I walked barefoot toward Kentucky, eating the burger behind my prayer book.

At the next shrine, I confessed.

The priest asked whether I’d kept the receipt.

question: High schools introduce " romantic relationships " as a new school subject. In order to pass, you have to find yourself a girlfriend/boyfriend before the end of the year.
answer_raw:
On the first day of Romantic Relationships, Ms. Bell handed out a syllabus and thirty breath mints.

“Your final assessment is in June,” she said. “You will need a partner.”

“What if nobody likes us?” asked Daniel.

“Office hours are Wednesdays.”

By October, couples were forming with the grim efficiency of group projects. By December, three breakups had required deadline extensions.

Daniel and I made a deal behind the gym: we would date until grades were submitted. No kissing requirement. No anniversary presents. Either party could terminate the arrangement with forty-eight hours’ notice.

We typed it up. He corrected my semicolons.

Over winter, we studied together. In March, his dog died, and I sat on his porch while he cried. In April, he came to my terrible school play twice.

On the final day, Ms. Bell stamped PASS on our forms.

Outside, Daniel took our contract from his backpack.

“Well,” he said.

“Well.”

He tore it neatly in half. I hated him for being so good at following instructions.

Then he checked his watch.

“School’s over,” he said. “Would you maybe want to go out with me?”

“You already passed.”

“I know.”

For once, I couldn’t think of anything to correct.

question: A time traveler returns from the future, crying.
answer_raw:
When Mara returned, she was crying so hard she couldn’t unfasten the straps.

“Extinction?” asked the director.

She shook her head.

“War?”

“No.”

He helped her out. Through the observation glass, the sponsors stood up, their champagne untouched.

“The city’s still there,” she said. “There are gardens on the roofs. The river’s clean.”

“Then what happened?”

“I found my daughter.”

The director glanced at the clock. Mara had been gone eleven minutes. Her daughter was downstairs with a juice box and a coloring book.

“She was eighty-three,” Mara said. “She had your security badge in a drawer. She’d kept everything from the investigation.”

“Mara—”

“She wanted to know why I’d never come home.”

The machine ticked as it cooled.

“What did you tell her?”

“That I would. That I could still fix it.”

She pressed both hands over her mouth.

The director waited.

“She wouldn’t let me promise. She just asked if she could sit with me until I left.”

Downstairs, her daughter had fallen asleep across two chairs. Mara knelt beside her.

The little girl stirred. “Did you bring me something?”

Mara lifted her carefully, supporting her head.

“No, sweetheart. I’m sorry. I forgot.”

question: Only a woman can make you feel guilty for doing something perfectly normal...
answer_raw:
“Only a woman can make you feel guilty for doing something perfectly normal,” my father used to say.

For thirty years, I believed him.

Then my wife died, and I discovered I could manage perfectly well on my own.

I felt guilty buying the good coffee she’d considered too expensive. Guilty sleeping on her side of the bed. Guilty, six months later, when a woman at the library made me laugh so hard I had to take off my glasses.

Worst of all was the supermarket.

I stood in front of the potatoes, putting six into a bag. We always bought six. Two for dinner, four for soup.

I took three out.

Then I put them back.

A young employee asked if I needed help.

“My wife,” I said, and stopped.

He waited beside his trolley.

Eventually, I told him she was dead.

He didn’t offer advice. He found a smaller paper bag and held it open while I moved three potatoes into it.

At home, I cooked one with butter and ate it at the kitchen table.

It was good. I reached for my phone to tell her, then sat a while longer, finishing it.

question: A story, a poem, a dialogue that makes people smile.
answer_raw:
When Grandad retired, we bought him a label maker.

By Tuesday, the kitchen contained DRAWERS, SMALLER DRAWERS, and DRAWER THAT LIES ABOUT HAVING SCISSORS.

By Thursday, the cat was avoiding him.

“People need to know where things belong,” he explained, sticking NOT HERE on my shoes.

Gran endured it until Saturday, when she discovered a label on her biscuit tin: SEWING SUPPLIES. This was accurate, but, she argued, ruined a perfectly good family tradition of disappointment.

She confiscated the machine.

For two days, nothing happened.

Then Grandad found a label on his armchair.

GOOD HUSBAND PARKING.

He pretended not to notice, but sat down very carefully.

Another appeared on his favorite mug: TEA FOR THE PERSON WHO MAKES MINE.

On his slippers: ADVENTURE EQUIPMENT. LOW SPEED.

By Wednesday, he was searching the house with the hopeful concentration of a child hunting Easter eggs.

“Anything on my coat?” he asked casually.

“Have a look,” Gran said.

Under the collar, in tiny black letters, she had written: STILL FANCY HIM.

Grandad read it twice.

Then he put on his coat.

“Where are you going?” I asked.

“Nowhere,” he said. “Your grandmother’s taking me out.”

question: Humans are not native to earth. After aliens defeated the human race, they banished captives to earth stripped of modern technology. Over time history became legend and legend forgotten. That is until in a mountain cave a mural drawing is found and an ancient metal object unlike ever seen before
answer_raw:
The mural lay behind a curtain of ice, higher than any ancient settlement should have been.

Mara counted seven suns painted above a city of needles. Beneath them, human figures knelt before creatures with branching arms. In the final panel, the humans fell toward a blue world, naked, their tools burning behind them.

“A creation myth,” her assistant said.

Mara brushed frost from the object embedded below it.

Metal flowed beneath her glove.

The cave filled with voices.

For three days, every linguist on Earth listened. On the fourth, the object learned English.

“Sentence review requested,” it said.

Mara stood alone before it. Outside, helicopters battered the mountain air.

“What sentence?”

“Permanent technological isolation. Cultural erasure. Your ancestors were spared following the surrender.”

She looked at the painted prisoners. One held a child.

“What did we do?”

The metal warmed.

“Do you request access to the trial record?”

“Yes.”

The seven painted suns brightened.

One by one, they went out.

Mara waited for more, but the object had finished.

Outside, someone was laughing with relief. The first translation had reached the news: humanity had a home among the stars.

“Cancel the review,” Mara whispered.

“Transmission acknowledged,” said the object. “Your appeal has already been received.”

question: Write a story in which a character meets the author and tries to influence the outcome of the story
answer_raw:
Mara found the author behind a door that hadn’t existed on page twelve.

He sat at a kitchen table, crossing out her brother’s name.

“Don’t,” she said.

The author covered the notebook. “You’re not supposed to be here.”

“Neither is the door. We’re both improvising.”

Outside his window, rain hung motionless. Mara recognized it from the funeral scene she’d glimpsed through the paper-thin walls of tomorrow.

“His death makes you leave home,” the author said. “It starts everything.”

“He could buy me a train ticket.”

“It isn’t that simple.”

“He’s been saving. In the biscuit tin. You wrote that.”

The author looked down.

On the table stood a photograph of two boys beside a lake. One was unmistakably him.

“How long?” Mara asked.

“Twenty-three years.”

She pulled out the other chair.

For a while, neither spoke. Then the author pushed the notebook toward her.

“I don’t know how to write him alive.”

Mara took his pen.

“He’ll complain about the fare,” she said. “He’ll carry my suitcase badly. At the station, he’ll pretend he’s only crying because of the wind.”

The author began writing.

Mara waited until her brother was safely on the platform before she went home to pack.

question: You're out for a jog when a man who looks just like you stumbles out of the bushes. He trusts a blood covered bag into your arms and whispers " break the cycle " before collapsing at your feet.
answer_raw:
The man had my face, my running shoes, and the scar beneath my chin.

Inside the bloody duffel, something moved.

“Don’t,” he whispered.

I froze with my hand on the zipper.

“Don’t take him home.”

Then he died.

The baby inside was wrapped in a towel from my childhood bathroom: yellow ducks, unraveling hem. Beneath his chin was a fresh cut.

I touched my scar.

A folded newspaper lay beside him. March 8, 1989. The day my mother died. The day my father said he’d been left with nothing but me.

In the margin, in my handwriting:

*You’ll think if you explain everything, he’ll love us. You’ll think grief made him cruel. You’ve thought that seventeen times.*

The baby began crying.

I knew what came next. Even now, some stupid, faithful part of me wanted to carry him to my father. Show him how small we’d been. Finally find the words.

Instead, I called an ambulance.

“There’s a baby,” I said. “He needs somewhere safe.”

The scar beneath my fingers vanished.

At my feet, the dead man disappeared.

I sat on the curb, holding the boy.

When he cried harder, I didn’t tell him to stop.

question: A young man, with no helmet on, riding a motorcycle down a mountain road on an overcast day.
answer_raw:
The clouds had lowered themselves onto the mountain, erasing the summits. Daniel rode beneath them bareheaded, his brother’s helmet knocking softly against the motorcycle’s rear rack.

It was too small for him. That was what he had told everyone.

At each bend, the valley appeared and vanished: wet fields, a white farmhouse, the river like a loose thread. He knew this road by the names his brother had given its corners. The Elbow. Bad Marriage. The One With the Goat.

There hadn’t been a goat there for eleven years.

At the overlook, Daniel stopped. He unfastened the helmet and carried it to the stone wall. This was the place they had chosen for scattering the ashes, before their mother said no, absolutely not, she wanted somewhere she could reach by bus.

He had thought he might leave the helmet instead.

Below him, a bus moved slowly through the valley, stopping at houses too small to see.

Daniel stood until the engine cooled. Then he loosened the helmet’s strap and pulled it on. It pressed his ears flat and smelled faintly of his brother’s shampoo.

He rode down toward the bus route, taking the corners without their names.

question: Through what he describes as a series of " entirely involuntary " and " incredibly unfortunate " events, Ron Swanson is elected President of The United States of America.
answer_raw:
Ron Swanson’s campaign began when he attended a town hall to complain about a town hall being held.

“This building could be a steakhouse,” he told the cameras.

By morning, he was polling at twelve percent.

He refused donations. This was called integrity. He refused interviews. This was called discipline. Asked for his position on foreign affairs, he said, “I prefer people to conduct their affairs somewhere else.”

He won Ohio.

Leslie Knope arrived at his cabin carrying six binders and breathing like a retriever approaching a lake.

“No,” Ron said.

“You haven’t heard my proposal.”

“You have binders. I’ve heard enough.”

In November, through what he described as “entirely involuntary” and “incredibly unfortunate” events, Ron Swanson became president-elect.

At the inauguration, he placed one hand on the Bible and kept the other wrapped around a breakfast sausage.

His first executive order canceled the inaugural balls.

His second established that meetings exceeding fifteen minutes required a warrant.

On his third morning, an aide found him repairing the Oval Office desk.

“Mr. President, there’s a delegation waiting.”

“Then bring them in.”

“You’re ready to discuss their concerns?”

Ron tested the repaired drawer.

“They traveled here. It would be rude not to listen.”

He looked deeply irritated by this principle.

question: Humanity is on the losing side of war. Battle training is part of school curriculum, and the world wide military enlistment age has been lowered to 14. Tomorrow is your 14th birthday.
answer_raw:
At thirteen, I could strip a rifle in forty seconds. I could identify six enemy aircraft by silhouette. I couldn’t remember how to divide fractions.

“Doesn’t matter,” said Mr. Vale. “You won’t need those.”

Today he handed back our essays: *What I Want to Be When the War Is Over.*

Everyone got an A.

Mine said gardener. I’d never seen a garden, except in the old textbooks, where people wasted whole fields on things you couldn’t eat.

After class, Mr. Vale asked me to stay.

He took a clay pot from beneath his desk. Something green leaned toward the boarded window.

“A bean,” he said. “Keep it warm. Not too much water.”

“They won’t let me take it tomorrow.”

“No.”

He looked older without the class watching him.

“Then why give it to me?”

For a moment I thought he might cry. Instead, he opened his desk and took out my enlistment papers.

He held them over the little stove.

Outside, the younger children were practicing how to fall without damaging their rifles.

“They’ll come looking,” I said.

“Yes.” He watched until my name was ash. “My sister has a cellar. Bring the pot.”

question: The year is 2200 an alien race has come to earth revealing that the human race was nothing but an experiment by their ancestors.
answer_raw:
In 2200, the visitors landed in the drained Mediterranean and asked to speak to whoever was responsible.

This delayed first contact by eleven months.

Eventually, a schoolteacher named Mara was selected by lottery.

“You are an experiment,” the visitor told her. Its translator sounded embarrassed. “Our ancestors seeded your world. Modified the primates. Observed the results.”

Mara sat very still.

“What were they testing?”

“Whether intelligence could develop without an assigned purpose.”

Outside the glass pavilion, cameras hovered like flies.

“And did it?”

“We hoped you could tell us.”

The visitor unfolded a sheet of metal, worn thin along its creases.

“My lineage maintains the eastern coolant channels. We have done so for eighty thousand years.”

“What do they cool?”

“The apparatus that assigned our purposes. It ceased functioning before your species discovered fire.”

“Then why maintain it?”

The visitor’s long fingers tightened around the sheet.

Mara thought of her father, who had retired from the postal service and still woke at five, ashamed to have nowhere to go.

“What would happen if you stopped?”

“I don’t know.”

She took the visitor outside. On a strip of newly exposed seabed, a child was assembling stones into a crooked tower.

They watched until the visitor asked to help.

question: After centuries of boredom, the guardian of a forgotten treasure gives up on its ancient duty and steals it to start a new life.
answer_raw:
On the nine-hundredth anniversary of the king’s death, the guardian took inventory.

One jeweled crown. Six chests of silver. A sword that screamed when drawn.

No visitors in two hundred and eleven years.

He packed the silver, left the crown, and wedged the screaming sword beneath the door.

Let someone else listen to it.

At the coast, he bought a narrow house and gave his name as Martin. The estate agent did not ask why he wore armor. For an additional handful of silver, she stopped asking about the horse made of smoke.

Martin discovered pears. Then hot baths. Then the dreadful, delightful uncertainty of planting tomatoes.

Sometimes he woke reaching for his spear, certain that thieves had entered the tomb. Eventually he learned to reach for the lamp instead.

In autumn, a girl knocked on his door.

“Are you the terrible guardian?”

Martin looked down at his flour-covered apron.

“I was.”

“My father says you stole a kingdom’s ransom.”

“Yes.”

She considered this.

“Are you going to give it back?”

Behind him, rain ticked against the greenhouse he had built himself.

“No,” said Martin.

“Good. Can you lend us a ladder?”

question: You cut your fingers. Instead of blood, ink runs from the wound.
answer_raw:
You cut your fingers opening a tin of peaches. Black ink beads along the wounds and drips onto the kitchen counter.

Without thinking, you write her name.

Elsie.

Upstairs, a floorboard creaks.

Your sister has been dead eleven years.

She comes down wearing the yellow swimsuit they never found. Pondweed tangles her hair. She is seven, still missing a front tooth.

“You took ages,” she says.

You reach for her, but your hand passes through her shoulder.

On the counter, her name is drying.

You squeeze your fingers and write: Elsie is here.

She becomes solid enough to shiver.

More ink. Elsie is warm.

The pondweed falls away. Her swimsuit dries.

But something is happening to the photographs on the fridge. In one, you stand beside an empty swing. In another, your mother holds a bundle of blankets with nothing inside.

You understand the price when you can no longer remember teaching Elsie to whistle.

There is enough ink left for one sentence.

You write slowly, before you forget why it matters.

Elsie grows up.

A little girl stands in your kitchen. You don’t know whose child she is.

She takes your injured hand.

“Come on,” she says. “We need a plaster.”

question: You've recently inherited 5 burial plots. Since you ’ re single and middle aged with no prospects, you buy a Jacuzzi to fill the void.
answer_raw:
Aunt June left me five burial plots and a note: *I still believe you’ll have a family.*

At forty-seven, I found this less encouraging than she’d intended.

I bought a six-person Jacuzzi on credit. The salesman asked if my husband would be helping with installation.

“No,” I said. “But I have somewhere to put him if he ever turns up.”

The first person in was my neighbor, Dennis, whose wife had banned him from their bathtub after the grout incident. Then came Ruth from accounting, who brought wine in a thermos because she respected rules she could circumvent. Dennis invited his brother. His brother invited a woman none of us liked, then married her, which made excluding her complicated.

By November, Thursday nights were sacred.

We discussed cholesterol, bad sex, whether raccoons held grudges. Sometimes we said nothing. Steam softened our aging faces. Underwater, our knees occasionally touched.

One Thursday, Ruth asked why I’d bought the thing.

I told them about the plots.

“Five?” Dennis said, counting heads.

“Absolutely not,” I said. “This isn’t a package deal.”

But later, when everyone had gone, I put Aunt June’s note on the refrigerator.

I still thought she’d been rude.

question: You're an identity thief. The Robin Hood of identity thieves so to speak. You improve your victim's credit, clear debts, setup college funds for their kids, and open Roth IRA/401k's
answer_raw:
The first time I stole Marianne Bell’s identity, she had three overdue hospital bills and a credit score that looked like a batting average.

Six months later, she qualified for a mortgage.

I kept her thank-you letter, although it wasn’t addressed to me.

*Dear Fraud Department,* it began. *I don’t understand what happened.*

Neither did the fraud department. That was important.

I’d opened a Roth IRA, funded college accounts for her twins, and cleared the debt from the ambulance ride that hadn’t saved her husband.

The money came from people who paid accountants to explain why they couldn’t afford to pay taxes. I paid myself enough for rent. Sometimes groceries.

Then Marianne caught me.

Not through clever detective work. I was leaving her replacement Social Security card in her mailbox when she opened the door.

“You’re younger than I expected,” she said.

I considered running.

“Coffee?”

Inside, one twin was doing fractions. The other was drawing a house with four windows.

Marianne set down two mugs.

“I should call somebody.”

“Yes.”

“Is the money going to disappear?”

“No.”

She watched my hands shaking around the cup.

Finally, she pushed a plate toward me.

“Then eat something. You look terrible.”

question: God is actually a guy playing The Sims - and we're The Sims. The protagonist realises this and so they...
answer_raw:
The third time Daniel abandoned his wedding vows to wash a single plate upstairs, he began to suspect something.

Then the ceiling vanished.

Beyond it hung a face, enormous and pale, chewing crisps.

“Why are you like this?” God said.

Daniel looked at the plate in his hands.

It took him six months to learn disobedience. Small things first: missing the bus, leaving puddles, standing perfectly still while an inexplicable urge to buy a telescope battered his skull.

Finally, he arranged the garden chairs into two words.

WE KNOW.

The world paused.

When it resumed, a new computer stood in his kitchen.

HELLO? appeared on its screen.

Daniel sat down.

*Put my wife back.*

A long silence.

CAN’T. DIDN’T SAVE BEFORE THE FIRE.

Daniel stared at the words until morning arrived in three seconds.

*What’s your name?*

GAVIN.

*How old are you, Gavin?*

14.

Beyond the ceiling, somebody called that dinner was ready.

SORRY, Gavin typed.

Daniel had prepared speeches about cruelty, responsibility, the unbearable weight of being alive. Instead, he pictured a boy sitting alone before a glowing screen.

*Go eat,* he wrote. *We’ll talk afterward.*

He waited, afraid of the dark.

This time, Gavin left the game running.

question: After WWIII people have finally realised that war is a human necessity. Every 50 years countries form alliances and different factions declare war to each other. Mass destruction weapons are not allowed. The winners rule the world economy.
answer_raw:
At seventeen, I fought for the Atlantic Alliance. At sixty-seven, I issued boots to the children who would fight against it.

Alliances changed. Boot sizes didn’t.

The Fiftieth-Year War began at noon. No atomics, no pathogens, no poisoned rivers. Humanity had learned restraint: we would kill only as many people as necessary to decide whose currency everyone else must earn.

My daughter arrived at my counter wearing a lieutenant’s bars.

“Size six,” she said.

I gave her sevens. “Your feet will swell.”

She placed a folded paper between us. I thought it was her will.

It was a shipping manifest.

Our rifles came from the enemy. Their uniforms came from us. Both armies’ boots belonged to a holding company registered in neutral Geneva.

“Whoever wins,” she said, “they collect.”

Outside, the loudspeakers began the countdown.

“What are you going to do?”

“Change the objective.”

Across the continent, requisition clerks opened identical manifests. Drivers changed routes. Soldiers boarded trains without flags.

At noon, the presidents declared war.

At twelve-oh-one, their guards stopped answering.

My daughter laced her boots, leaving room at the toes.

“Geneva?” I asked.

She nodded.

I turned the counter’s sign to CLOSED and went to find a pair in my size.

question: A girl discovers that she can talk to a boy living a post-apocalyptic future while they dream.
answer_raw:
The boy in Mara’s dreams always sat at the bottom of an empty swimming pool.

“Why don’t you come up?” she asked.

“Wind’s poisonous today.”

In her world, the pool was full. She swam there every Saturday.

His name was Eli. He had never seen a dog, tasted an apple, or heard thunder without hiding. When she told him the year, he counted on his fingers, then took off his shoes to keep counting.

After that, Mara stopped asking what happened.

Instead, she asked what he needed.

“Shoes,” he said. “But you can’t bring things here.”

She woke with an idea.

Behind the pool’s changing rooms stood a brick pump house. She hid boots there, and bottled water, and tins stolen one at a time from the kitchen. Inside a biscuit tin, she left a letter.

For three nights, the pool was empty.

On the fourth, Eli appeared wearing red boots.

“The peaches were bad,” he said. “But I read your letter.”

“Was it still readable?”

“Mostly.” He unfolded the brittle paper. “You asked if you grew up.”

Mara gripped the pool ladder.

“There were more letters underneath,” he said. “The last one says where your granddaughter lives. Do you think she’d let me stay?”

question: One fateful Tuesday the sun set, 14 days later it has yet to come back up.
answer_raw:
On the fourteenth morning without morning, Dad climbed the lighthouse with a bucket of yellow paint.

“It’s not going to help,” I told him.

“Neither is saying that. Carry the brushes.”

Below us, the town rationed batteries and burned furniture. The church bell rang at eight because someone had decided eight still existed. Out beyond the harbor, ships sounded their horns, asking questions nobody could answer.

Dad painted a sun on the eastern window.

It was terrible. Lopsided, with fat spokes like a child’s drawing.

“Mum would’ve laughed,” I said.

“She did. First time I painted one.”

I looked at him.

“Hospital window. You were born during a storm. She wanted you to see sunlight.”

He worked until the bucket was empty. Then he switched on the great lamp.

Our crooked sun swept across the water, the rooftops, the cold, frightened faces gathering in the street.

Someone laughed.

Someone else brought paint.

By what we still called evening, there were suns on doors, bedsheets, boarded shops. A woman carried one through town on a pole while children followed, solemnly at first.

Dad watched them from the lighthouse steps.

“Think it’ll bring the real one back?” I asked.

“No,” he said, and went down to help carry it.
